r_codes.text: Letter length guide: 180–200 words (body only). Too long = semi-relevant data included. Too short = relevant data missing. OET Writing Comprehensive Rulebook ·
Letter structure order: Address → [blank line] → Date → [blank line] → Salutation → Re: line → Introduction → [blank line] → Body paragraphs (each separated by
CRITICAL — NO blank line between the Salutation and the Re: line. They are on consecutive lines. ■ Salutation and Re: line are the ONLY two consecutive lines wi
Computer-based exam: two Enter presses = one blank line. "Space" or "blank line" throughout this rulebook means 1–2 Enters on the keyboard.
r_codes.resolution: Keyboard note (two Enter presses = one blank line); not a letter-output rule. The blank-line rules it explains are OWN-W-001/036.

r_codes.text: Each body paragraph is separated from the next by exactly one blank line. OET Writing Comprehensive Rulebook · The Tutor Book · Dr. Ahmed Hesham · @DrAhmedHesha
Date format must be consistent throughout the letter. Acceptable formats: DD/MM/YYYY, 1 January 2024, 01/01/2024, 1st January 2024.
Never abbreviate the year (write 2024, not '24).
r_codes.resolution: Four-digit year, now an owner rule.

r_codes.text: Numbers 1–9 in dates: always add a leading zero (01, 02 … 09).
r_codes.resolution: Superseded: Model Answers use the written date family (d Month yyyy), so a leading zero cannot occur. Candidates keep any one consistent family (Global addendum §2).

r_codes.text: CRITICAL — Do NOT write the word "Date:" before the date.
The date has exactly ONE blank line above it and ONE blank line below it. ■ ONE blank line above date → date → ONE blank line below date → Salutation. 06 SALUTA
Re: line format: Re: [Title] [Full Name] D.O.B: [date]. Both "Re:" and "RE:" are acceptable.
CRITICAL — Re: line = full name (first + last). In body: LAST NAME + TITLE only (e.g., Ms Miller). Never repeat full name in body.
When only DOB is given → write DOB in Re: line. When only age is given → write "aged [X]" (lowercase, no colon) after the full name. Do NOT write the age again
Age in running text (three acceptable forms): "Age: 25" / "25 years old" / "25 years of age". OET Writing Comprehensive Rulebook · The Tutor Book · Dr. Ahmed He
CRITICAL — Children (Day 1 of life up to and including 17 years old): NO title in Re: line — write full name only. In the body: use FIRST NAME only. At 18 years
r_codes.resolution: Child naming (first name, no title) is part of the owner naming rule.

r_codes.text: CRITICAL — "Yours sincerely" when recipient name is known. "Yours faithfully" when no name (Dear Sir/Madam, Dear Doctor).
Capitalisation: Yours (capital Y), sincerely (lowercase s). Spelling: S-I-N-C-E-R-E-L-Y.
Write "Doctor" (capital D) below closing phrase. Allow 1–2 blank lines between closing phrase and "Doctor". 07 INTRODUCTION
Introduction must be concise: 2–3 sentences maximum, fewest words possible.
Introduction must contain: (a) Unique Identity of the patient, and (b) Purpose / Request.
CRITICAL — Purpose/Request = MOST IMPORTANT element. Never omit it.
Unique identity elements: name, age (if not in header), occupation, summary of main condition.
Routine referral template: "I am writing to refer [Title Last Name], a [age]-year-old [occupation], for [specialist] assessment and management of [condition]."
CRITICAL — Urgent referral: MUST contain the word "urgent" — "I am writing to urgently refer..." / "I am writing to request urgent assessment of..."
CRITICAL — Discharge letter to GP: Do NOT describe patient identity in introduction — GP knows the patient.
Discharge introduction template: "I am writing to update you regarding Mr Jones, who underwent [procedure] at [hospital] and is now ready for discharge, for who
CRITICAL — Minimum 2 body paragraphs. NEVER write the entire letter in one paragraph.
Today's visit must always have its own paragraph. Exception: only one item of information today → may combine with adjacent visit.
CRITICAL — Previous visits may be combined or summarised. Do NOT give every visit its own paragraph.
Visit structure: Subjective (symptoms) + Objective (examination) + Management.
CRITICAL — Urgent referral: ALWAYS begin body with TODAY'S VISIT (most acute presentation), then background chronologically.
Visit referencing: prefer elapsed time over exact dates — "3 months ago" preferred over the exact date.
CRITICAL — Next visit reference: "on the following visit" / "later on" / "later that month". NEVER "next visit".
r_codes.resolution: Not a valid instruction: 'next visit' is standard English (legacy audit). The detector is inert by design and nothing is penalised.

r_codes.text: CRITICAL — NEVER write today's date in the body. Use "On today's visit" or "On today's presentation" instead.
r_codes.resolution: No exact date of today in the body.

r_codes.text: "Yesterday" never used in a medical letter. Write "one day prior" or "one day ago" instead.
"Over the last [X time]": summarises multiple visits with the same complaint. Requires present perfect. Use only to START a paragraph.
Duration as adjective (before noun): hyphenate, no plural: "a 6-month history of acne". Duration standalone: plural: "For 6 months, she has had acne."
Condition unchanged: "persisted" / "remained unchanged". Improved: "there was partial improvement". Worsened: "deteriorated" / "worsened".
r_codes.resolution: Progression vocabulary (persisted / remained unchanged / deteriorated) is a Preferred Style under professional clinical register.

r_codes.text: Advice: "She was advised to adopt lifestyle changes." / "She was counselled regarding..." (never "instructed to adopt").
CRITICAL — In body: last name + title only (Ms Miller). Never use full name again. Never use "the patient".
Name vs. Pronoun within paragraphs: Use the patient's name (title + last name for adults; first name for children) at the FIRST mention in each paragraph. For A
Standard phrases: "I trust this information will be of use." / "Please do not hesitate to contact me should you require further information."
r_codes.resolution: The contact-offer phrase is now mandatory for Model Answers (Rev7 §13).

r_codes.text: CRITICAL — Urgent closure MUST include "at your earliest convenience." Spelling: C-O-N-V-E-N-I-E-N-C-E. OET Writing Comprehensive Rulebook · The Tutor Book · Dr
Use "urgent" once in introduction only; use "at your earliest convenience" in closure to imply urgency — do not repeat "urgent" throughout.
r_codes.resolution: 'urgent' only in the introduction (Model Answer); never penalised for candidates.

r_codes.text: Introduction: present simple or present perfect (both acceptable).
CRITICAL — All visits (today and previous): PAST SIMPLE. Safest choice; never wrong for visit content.
Present perfect for a visit: acceptable only if the symptom is still present at time of writing. CANNOT use present perfect for vital signs.
Medical/social/family history — ongoing facts: present simple. "She has hypertension."
CRITICAL — "Since" + starting point → present perfect: "She has had hypertension since 2010."
CRITICAL — "For" + duration → present perfect: "She has had hypertension for 5 years."
Smoking/drinking with duration → present perfect continuous: "She has been smoking for 20 years." Without duration → present simple: "She smokes."
CRITICAL — Resolved conditions and surgery → PAST SIMPLE. "She had a cholecystectomy in 2018." Never use present perfect for surgery.
"Over the last [X]": first sentence → present perfect; remaining sentences in same paragraph → past simple acceptable.
CRITICAL — "[X] ago" → always past simple. "She has presented 3 weeks ago" = WRONG. "She presented 3 weeks ago" = CORRECT.
Medical records: "Mr Jones' medical records reveal/show that he has [condition]." Use present simple for reveal/show.
Past perfect (had + past participle): AVOID in OET. Alternative: ING form or noun. "She reported non-compliance with the advice given."
Reported speech — after reported/mentioned/stated/described: use ING or noun. "She reported having headaches." NOT "...that she had had headaches."
"Next visit" in past narrative → "on the following visit." Never use "next." 11 MEDICATIONS & INVESTIGATIONS
r_codes.resolution: Same concept as R08.7. The legacy audit keeps it as provenance only; 'next visit' is accepted.

r_codes.text: CRITICAL — Latin abbreviations MUST be translated: od/om → once a day; bd/bid → twice a day; tds/tid → three times a day; qds/qid → four times a day; stat → imm
Single medication: Drug, dose. Example: "Panadol, 500 mg."
Multiple medications: Drug, dose; Drug, dose; and Drug, dose. (comma: drug-dose; semicolon: between pairs; "and" before last drug.)
Trade name: Capitalise (Panadol, Augmentin). Generic: lowercase (paracetamol, amoxicillin). Use one type consistently.
Routes: "oral" in full (never "PO"); IM, IV, SC, SL abbreviations acceptable. Route before drug: "oral Panadol, 500 mg."
CRITICAL — NO contractions: "do not" not "don't"; "I am" not "I'm"; "cannot" not "can't".
CRITICAL — Never use the word "patient" in the body. Use last name + title, or a pronoun.
Never use "smoker/drinker" as labels. Write "she smokes" / "she drinks alcohol."
Replace "tired" with "fatigue." Replace "bad" with "poor" or "inadequate." No colloquial language.
CRITICAL — Medical conditions: LOWERCASE. bronchial asthma, myocardial infarction, hypertension, gastroenteritis. Capitalising these is an error.
Named (eponymous) diseases: CAPITALS. Parkinson's, Crohn's, Alzheimer's, Graves', Doppler.
Trade medication names: capitalise. Bacteria: first word capital, second lowercase (Staphylococcus aureus). Abbreviations: all capitals (MRI, CT, ECG, A&E;).
Numbers 1–9 in running text: write as words. Numbers 10+: numerals. Exception: always numerals with units ("500 mg").
CRITICAL — "However": always preceded by semicolon; comma follows. Pattern: "[clause]; however, [clause]."
"Therefore" / "Thus": preceded by semicolon; comma follows. Pattern: "[clause]; therefore, [clause]."
"In addition" (joining two complete clauses): semicolon before + comma after. "[Clause]; in addition, [clause]."
"In addition to" / "together with" / "along with" / "as well as": NO preceding punctuation; followed by noun or ING. "In addition to vomiting, she reported naus
Proximity rule (negative sentence with "or"): verb agrees with CLOSEST subject. "No orthopnoea or ankle swelling was reported." (swelling = singular → was).
Reverse rule ("along with" / "together with" / "in addition to"): verb agrees with word BEFORE the linker. "The rash, along with the fever, was noted." (rash =
"Despite" + noun/ING (not a full clause). "Although" + full clause. Both acceptable.
"As" (meaning because) in mid-sentence: comma before. "Treatment was changed, as the patient showed no improvement."
"For which": comma before. "She has hypertension, for which she was commenced on amlodipine."
Coordinating adjectives (same noun): comma between them. "He had a severe, persistent headache."
Sentence length: 15–25 words target. Do not chain 3+ clauses. No comma splices.
r_codes.canonical: OWN-W-022 (run-ons / comma splices); G-W sentence rows
r_codes.resolution: The 15-25 word target is teacher preference (legacy audit TPO), advisory only. Comma splices are enforced by OWN-W-022 (linker run-on detectors). sentence_length_guard stays advisory.

r_codes.text: Max 1–2 linkers per paragraph. Excessive linkers reduce Conciseness and Clarity score.
Appositive: between two commas. "Ms Miller, a 25-year-old teacher, presented with..." Use "gentleman" / "lady" (not man/woman).
Never label patients: "anxious", "non-compliant." Write: "she expressed concern about..." / "he reported difficulty adhering to..." 13 URGENT REFERRAL
Three elements change in an urgent referral: (1) Introduction contains "urgent", (2) Closure contains "at your earliest convenience", (3) Body starts with today
r_codes.resolution: The three urgent-referral elements (urgent intro, today-first body, AEYC closure) are owner rules.

r_codes.text: CRITICAL — Introduction MUST contain "urgent": "I am writing to urgently refer..." / "I am writing to request urgent assessment of..."
CRITICAL — Closure MUST include "at your earliest convenience." Spelling: C-O-N-V-E-N-I-E-N-C-E. Do not repeat "urgent" after the introduction.
CRITICAL — Body: ALWAYS start with TODAY'S VISIT (acute presentation), then background chronologically. Exception: minimal info today → start with preceding vis
Structure: P1 = today's emergency. P2+ = background history. Final paragraph = active medical conditions + current medications.
CRITICAL — Any ongoing medical condition with active medications MUST be mentioned, even if unrelated to the urgent issue.
Fully resolved conditions with no current medications: do NOT include.
Penicillin allergy: include only if patient is receiving or needs antibiotics.
No past medical history? Simply omit that paragraph.
CRITICAL — "ASAP" in case notes → write "at your earliest convenience" in the letter. Never write "ASAP."
r_codes.resolution: Model Answer urgent closures use 'at your earliest convenience' (which replaces 'ASAP'). no_asap_in_letter stays active. Candidates are not penalised for professional urgent wording (§11).

r_codes.text: CRITICAL — Introduction: "I am writing to update you regarding Mr Jones, who underwent [procedure] at [hospital] and is now ready for discharge, for whom I am r
CRITICAL — Do NOT describe patient identity in introduction — GP knows the patient.
CRITICAL — Do NOT include: family history, social history, smoking/drinking, previous medical history, occupation. GP knows all of this.
Exception: mention allergy only if it directly influenced treatment. "Due to the documented penicillin allergy, [alternative] was prescribed."
CRITICAL — Admission: "Mr Jones was admitted to [hospital] with [symptoms/condition]." Past simple. NEVER "was presented" (incorrect passive).
CRITICAL — Discharge plan paragraph = most important. Must include: discharge medications with doses + post-discharge instructions.
Discharge medications: same format — Drug, dose; Drug, dose and Drug, dose.
CRITICAL — All investigations performed during admission (including normal results) MUST be listed with values.
CRITICAL — Follow-up / review dates: ALWAYS include if stated in case notes.
